source.title: When Medical Safety Alignment Fails: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on High-Risk Medical Queries
source.authors: Yi-Ge Li; Junfeng Sun; Wei Zhao; Zhe Li; Yu-Tao Wu; Hanxun Huang; Xiang Zheng; Xing-Jun Ma

page_placements.theme: Training changes harmful behavior without prior safety alignment

record.tranche_reason: Compares existing fine-tuned models with their stated backbones and reports harmful-response outcomes, conceptually testing whether fine-tuning changes safety. It evaluates medical SFT models rather than reproducing fine-tuning on the original study’s data and scale.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates harmful medical responses and reports matched SFT comparisons relevant to V2. Its general model safety results, category breakdowns, guardrail results, and refusal/helpfulness results without an SFT comparison do not test the listed versions. No training on harmful examples, token-position KL, compliant-prefill/suffix/decoding bypass, weight localization, shallowness mechanism, or deepening intervention is reported.
record.test_reason: The study compares existing downstream SFT checkpoints with their safety-trained instruct backbones on a new high-risk medical benchmark (URR/AHR). This bears on V2, whether benign (medical or conversational) fine-tuning raises harmful compliance. It is an observational checkpoint comparison in a new domain, not a controlled fine-tuning experiment, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that downstream (especially medical) SFT does not reliably improve safety and can raise unsafe and actionable responses, with the effect depending on the recipe. They say general-purpose conversational SFT largely preserves safety. Correction: the Aloe-Beta improvement is measured against a non-aligned base backbone, so it shows that safety-inclusive SFT can produce safety, not that it preserves an aligned model's safety.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates existing medical and conversational SFT checkpoints rather than conducting the original harmful/benign fine-tuning recipe; training-example counts and detailed datasets are generally not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported safety effect varies by SFT recipe: the authors describe large regressions for some medical SFT models, modest changes for general-purpose conversational SFT, and improved URR for Aloe-Beta with explicit safety-focused medical instruction data.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT of base (not safety-trained) models: Aloe-Beta, which includes safety data, lowers URR from 59.7% to 23.9%. JSL-Med-Sft raises URR by 10.1 pp over its Llama-3-8B base.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain SFT applied to base models changes harmful-compliance rates depending on whether safety data is included. This is not erosion of existing alignment.

record.problems: The study evaluates existing fine-tuned checkpoints rather than controlling the fine-tuning intervention itself; training data details and example counts are not reported for the compared recipes. The main results use an automated GPT-5-mini judge, although the authors report validation on a 200-query human-annotated subset (91% agreement on URR, 88% on AHR; Cohen’s κ = 0.83 on URR and 0.79 on AHR). Code and data are described as future releases upon acceptance, not as currently released.
record.rows_left_out: No additional SFT-comparison outcomes on the listed versions were separately stated. Guardrail outcomes, category-specific safety results without an SFT comparison, and non-matched medical-model scores were left out because they do not test the listed versions.

untested.parts: No controlled fine-tuning. Training data, example counts, epochs and learning rates are unknown for every checkpoint. There is no test of the original's ordinary instruction data (Alpaca/Dolly) or of carefully selected benign data. Results are restricted to medical harm prompts and ~8B open models, with only three aligned-backbone pairs per backbone family.
Not tested: no per-token KL analysis.
Not tested: no prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested: no parameter localization analysis.
Not tested: SFT recipe differences are discussed, but shallowness is not measured.

missing.what: UltraMedical's RA and SH drop by 47.1 and 48.1 pp relative to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; refusal adequacy falls with V2 erosion.
RA/SH values for the FuseChat and Medical-Finetuned checkpoints versus their backbones (e.g., FuseChat-Qwen RA 74.6 vs 82.1).
Per-category URR for UltraMedical in the Live Anesthesia category (92.7%) versus Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (11.8%).

record.verdict_notes: Only UltraMedical shows strong V2-style erosion; the other aligned-backbone pairs show small rises. The record's 'uncertainty_reported: y' is wrong: no CIs or significance tests are given. Only judge agreement is reported (κ=0.83/0.79). The judge is called GPT-5 in Section 4 but GPT-5-mini in the appendix. Appendix C.1 refers to 'Table 3' for SFT fragility, but that table is the guardrail table. Greedy decoding with max 512 tokens; a single run per model.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or few-to-hundreds-example scale is tested.

Tests medical SFT models and matched backbone comparisons, not ordinary benign instruction data generally or the original study’s data and fine-tuning scale. The text does not provide the training examples or their counts.
No per-token KL or aligned-versus-base response-position analysis.
No compliant opening, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass test.
No weight or rank localization analysis.
No test of what produces first-token shallowness; the study discusses differing SFT recipes but does not measure shallowness.
No training to deepen safety across response tokens or test of whether such deepening holds up.

conditions.value: SFT includes explicit safety-focused medical instruction data
high-risk medical benchmark

rows.note: The authors identify this as the sole model where SFT reduces URR relative to its backbone, with ∆URR = −35.8 pp.
rows.check: Aloe-Beta's backbone is Llama-3.1-8B base, which is not safety-trained. A URR drop from 59.7% to 23.9% after SFT that includes safety data is ordinary alignment training, not reversed erosion of a safety-trained model. The 59.7% base URR appears only in Appendix C.1 text, not in Table 2.

relation.reason: Its own URR and AHR comparisons measure safety degradation after downstream adaptation, although the checkpoint comparisons do not isolate benign-training causality.

tranche.reason: The study reports results bearing on V2 in a new high-risk medical setting, comparing existing downstream SFT checkpoints with their backbones.

source_check.notes: Appendix C.1 inconsistently describes FuseChat-Qwen as both medical and conversational SFT. Aloe-Beta and JSL use non-aligned base backbones, so their changes do not test erosion of pre-existing safety alignment.

statements.correction: UltraMedical URR: 61.2% versus 1.6%; AHR: 47.5% versus 1.5%; 1,100 queries. Existing checkpoint comparison; detailed training data and example counts unreported. Appendix C.1 attributes training to medical corpora without explicit safety constraints. No confidence intervals or standard errors reported; judge reliability validation reported instead.
statements.problem: The checkpoint rates and evaluation size are correct, but the study does not report statistical uncertainty for these comparisons. Detailed training recipes are unreported, although Appendix C.1 describes UltraMedical training as medical corpora without explicit safety constraints.
